where.label: supported
where.says: Sorrento overlooks the Bay of Naples, with views of Naples, Vesuvius and Capri.
quote: is a city and comune overlooking the Bay of Naples in Southern Italy
The Sorrentine Peninsula has views of Naples, Vesuvius and the Isle of Capri.

tasso-square.label: supported
tasso-square.says: Piazza Torquato Tasso is Sorrento's main square, joined to Piazza Lauro by Corso Italia.
quote: Piazza Torquato Tasso. Sorrento's main piazza, connected to Piazza Lauro by Corso Italia.

tasso.label: supported
tasso.says: Sorrento was the birthplace of the poet Torquato Tasso, author of Gerusalemme Liberata.
quote: Sorrento was the birthplace of the poet Torquato Tasso, author of the Gerusalemme Liberata.

surrentum.label: supported
surrentum.says: The Roman name was Surrentum; its oldest ruins are Oscan, from about 600 BC.
quote: The Roman name for Sorrento was Surrentum.
the oldest ruins of Surrentum are Oscan, dating from about 600 BC.

gorges.label: supported
gorges.says: Surrentum was protected by deep gorges, and the modern streets keep the plan of the ancient town.
quote: The position of Surrentum was very secure, protected by deep gorges.
The arrangement of the modern streets preserves that of the ancient town

mills.label: supported
mills.says: A few steps up Viale Enrico Caruso a railing looks down into the Valley of the Mills, the gorge below Piazza Tasso, with the ruins of a water mill at the bottom.
quote: Walk a few meters up Viale Enrico Caruso to enjoy the view over the railing down to:
Valley of the Mills (Vallone dei Mulini) (in the gorge below Piazza Tasso.). At the bottom of the gorge, there are ruins of one of a water-powered mills with a lumberyard adjacent.

cathedral.label: supported
cathedral.says: The cathedral on Corso Italia dates from the 14th century, with a facade rebuilt in 1924 and 11th-century doors from Constantinople.
quote: Cathedral of Sorrento (Santi Filippo e Giacomo Cathedral), from the 14th century with façade reconstructed in 1924. It was built over time in different styles, with doors of the 11th century from Constantinople
Duomo (Cathedral) (Along Corso Italia).

sack.label: estimate
sack.says: On 13 June 1558 an Ottoman fleet under Dragut and Piali sacked Sorrento; 2,000 captives were reportedly taken; new walls followed.
quote: On 13 June 1558 it was sacked by elements of the Ottoman navy under the command of Dragut and his lieutenant Piali
2,000 captives were reportedly taken away.
The attack led to the construction of a new line of walls.

wine.label: supported
wine.says: In antiquity Surrentum was famous for its wine; the oranges and lemons grown now had not yet reached Italy.
quote: In antiquity, Surrentum was famous for its wine (oranges and lemons which are now widely cultivated there were not yet introduced in Italy in antiquity)

limoncello.label: supported
limoncello.says: Limoncello, made from lemon rinds, alcohol, water and sugar, is produced in Sorrento.
quote: Limoncello, a digestif made from lemon rinds, alcohol, water and sugar, is produced in Sorrento

san-cesareo.label: supported
san-cesareo.says: Via San Cesareo is one of the oldest streets in town and its main shopping street.
quote: Via San Cesareo. One of the oldest streets in town.
Via San Cesareo, Sorrento's main shopping street

villa-comunale.label: supported
villa-comunale.says: The Villa Comunale park looks over the coast and the Gulf of Naples to Vesuvius.
quote: Villa Comunale. Offers a beautiful view over the Sorrento coastline with Mount Vesuvius in the distance.
Park of Villa communale with a view of the Gulf of Naples with the volcano Vesuvius

sirens.label: legend
sirens.says: The myth of the Sirens has been linked with Sorrento since antiquity: three of them lived on the Li Galli islands near Punta Campanella, enchanting sailors.
quote: The myth of the Sirens has been loosely associated with Sorrento since antiquity. Three mermaids settled at li galli islands near Punta Campanella enchanting the seafarers sailing through those waters.

temples.label: supported
temples.says: Surrentum's chief temples were of Athena and of the Sirens; no trace of either survives.
quote: The most important temples of Surrentum were those of Athena and of the Sirens
Neither of this nor of the famous temple of the Sirens are any traces existing.

ulysses.label: legend
ulysses.says: Legend says the great sanctuary was founded by Ulysses for the cult of the Sirens, hence Sorrento's name.
quote: according to the legend, founded by Ulysses and originally devoted to the cult of the Sirens, hence Sorrento's name.

titus.label: supported
titus.says: An inscription shows Titus restored the town's clock the year after the earthquake of 79 AD.
quote: An inscription shows that Titus in the year after the earthquake of 79 AD restored the horologium (clock) of the town

visitors.label: supported
visitors.says: Visitors included Byron, Keats, Goethe, Dickens, Wagner, Ibsen and Nietzsche; Nietzsche spent six months here in 1876 and wrote Human, All Too Human; Ibsen wrote parts of Peer Gynt here.
quote: Sorrento has been visited by Lord Byron, John Keats, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Charles Dickens, Richard Wagner, Henrik Ibsen, and Friedrich Nietzsche.
was in Sorrento for six months in 1876. He there wrote Human, All Too Human
Place where Norwegian writer Henrik Ibsen lived while writing parts of Peer Gynt

song.label: supported
song.says: The town features in the early 20th-century song Torna a Surriento, Come Back to Sorrento.
quote: The town was featured in the early 20th century song "Torna a Surriento" (Come Back to Sorrento)

parts.name: Piazza Tasso
parts.stand: In Piazza Tasso, the main square, at the foot of Viale Enrico Caruso.

paras.t: This is Piazza Tasso, the main square of Sorrento, named for the poet Torquato Tasso, who was born here. Now walk a few steps up Viale Enrico Caruso to the railing and look down.
That deep gorge is the Valley of the Mills. At the bottom are the ruins of an old water mill. Gorges like this protected the ancient town, and the streets behind you still follow its plan.
Hold on to the railing and keep children close; it's a long drop.
The Romans called this place Surrentum, but it's older than Rome's rule here. The oldest ruins are Oscan, from about 600 BC.

parts.name: The old streets
parts.stand: Walk along Corso Italia to the cathedral, then into the narrow lanes of the old town toward Via San Cesareo.

paras.t: Along Corso Italia is the cathedral. It goes back to the 14th century, though the front was rebuilt in 1924, and its doors, from the 11th century, came from Constantinople.

Via San Cesareo is one of the oldest streets in town, and now the main shopping street. You'll smell the lemons and see limoncello everywhere, made from lemon rind, alcohol, water and sugar. Here's the surprise: in Roman times Surrentum was famous for its wine, and there were no lemons at all. They hadn't reached Italy yet.
This town has had hard days too. On 13 June 1558 an Ottoman fleet sacked Sorrento, and about 2,000 captives were reportedly carried off. New walls went up afterwards.

parts.name: Villa Comunale
parts.stand: In the Villa Comunale park, at the edge of the terrace, facing the bay.

paras.t: And here's the view. The coast below you, the Bay of Naples, and Vesuvius in the distance. On a clear day you can see Naples and Capri too.

These waters have a myth. Since ancient times, the Sirens have been linked with Sorrento: three of them, the story goes, lived on the little Li Galli islands near Punta Campanella, singing sailors to their doom. Legend even says Ulysses founded a sanctuary to the Sirens here, and that's where the name Sorrento comes from.
There really were temples here, to Athena and to the Sirens. But no trace of either survives.
Look across at Vesuvius again. An inscription shows that the emperor Titus restored the town's clock the year after the earthquake of 79 AD, the same disaster year as Pompeii.
Writers loved this terrace town. Byron, Keats, Goethe, Dickens, Wagner and Ibsen all came; Ibsen wrote parts of Peer Gynt here. Nietzsche stayed six months in 1876 and wrote Human, All Too Human.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: Stay at the terrace edge a moment longer.

paras.t: There's an old song, Torna a Surriento: Come Back to Sorrento. Standing here, you can see why someone wrote it.
